chapters.n: Third Nephi opens about 1 BC, exactly 600 years after Lehi left Jerusalem. This milestone matters because Lehi prophesied the Messiah would come 600 years after his departure.
Nephi, son of Helaman, hands the sacred records, including the brass plates, to his eldest son, also named Nephi, who becomes the main record keeper and namesake of this book.
The elder Nephi then leaves, and no one knows where he went, a quiet and mysterious exit reminiscent of Alma’s.

f.w: whither he went, no man knoweth

chapters.n: As the ninety-second year begins, prophecies are being fulfilled more and more, with greater signs and miracles.
But some claim the deadline for Samuel’s prophecy has passed.
They mock the believers: Samuel’s words have failed, so your joy and faith were for nothing.
The unbelievers make a great uproar, and believers grow anxious that the prophecy might not come true.
Even so, the faithful keep watching steadily for the promised day, night, and day without darkness.
The unbelievers set a date: if the sign has not come by then, all believers will be put to death. Faith now carries a deadly price.
Nephi, son of Nephi, is heartbroken at his people’s wickedness.
He goes out, bows to the ground, and prays mightily for the believers about to be killed for their faith.
He prays all day long, and then the Lord’s voice comes to him.

“Lift up your head and be of good cheer.” The sign will come tonight, and tomorrow the Lord will be born into the world, fulfilling everything His prophets said. Jesus Christ Himself speaks on the eve of His own birth.

f.w: on the morrow come I into the world

chapters.n: He comes to His own to fulfill all things and do the will of the Father and the Son. He is called “the Father” because of His divine role and “the Son” because He takes on a body of flesh.

f.w: of the Father because of me, and of the Son because of my flesh

chapters.n: The Lord’s words are fulfilled. At sunset no darkness comes, and people are astonished as night falls without dark.
Many unbelievers fall to the ground as if dead. They realize their plan to kill the believers has been foiled.
Everyone across the land, north and south, east and west, falls to the earth in amazement, knowing the Son of God must soon appear.
They remember the long years of prophecy and are afraid because of their sins and unbelief.
The whole night stays as bright as noon. In the morning the sun rises normally, and they know this is the day the Lord is born.

f.w: as light as though it was mid-day

chapters.n: Everything happens exactly as the prophets said, to the last detail.
A new star also appears, as foretold, matching the star seen by the wise men in the East.
Satan immediately spreads lies to make people doubt what they saw, but most believe and turn to the Lord.
Nephi and others baptize many unto repentance, bringing widespread forgiveness, and peace returns.

f.g: Forgiveness; cancellation of the debt of sin.

chapters.n: A minor dispute arises: some argue from scripture that the law of Moses no longer needs to be kept. They misunderstood, because Christ had been born but had not yet fulfilled the law through His atonement.
They are soon corrected: the law must be fulfilled completely, not one “jot or tittle” passing away until then. They admit their error.

f.g: The smallest Hebrew letter (yod) and a tiny pen-stroke; the smallest detail.

chapters.n: The ninety-second year ends with joy because the holy prophets’ words have come true.
The ninety-third year is peaceful, except for the Gadianton robbers in the mountains, whose strongholds are too strong to conquer and who murder many.
In the ninety-fourth year the robbers grow greatly as Nephite dissenters flee to them, bringing sorrow to the faithful.
The Lamanites grieve too: many of their young people, growing up and becoming independent, are lured by the lies and flattery of Zoramites into joining the robbers.

f.g: Became independent; made their own choices.

chapters.n: So the Lamanites suffer as well, and their faith and righteousness decline because of the wickedness of the rising generation. Each generation must choose faith for itself.

Only a few years after the miraculous night without darkness, people begin to forget. Signs that once amazed them now seem ordinary, and their hearts harden and minds grow blind. Spiritual experiences fade if not nurtured.

f.w: began to forget those signs and wonders

chapters.n: They explain away the signs as human tricks or the devil’s work. Satan regains control and convinces them the doctrine of Christ is foolish.
Wickedness grows. People decide there will be no more signs, and Satan leads them into great sin.
Years pass, the ninety-sixth through ninety-ninth of the judges.
A century has passed since King Mosiah, who ended the monarchy and set up the reign of judges.
And 609 years have passed since Lehi left Jerusalem.
It has been nine years since the sign of Christ’s birth.
The Nephites change their calendar to count from the sign of Christ’s coming. Much as the later Christian world would date years from His birth, the Nephites center time on Christ.

f.g: Count their years; keep their calendar.

chapters.n: The elder Nephi, father of the record keeper, never returns and cannot be found anywhere.
Despite much preaching and prophecy, the people remain wicked through the tenth and eleventh years.
By the thirteenth year, the Gadianton robbers are so numerous and destructive, killing many and wasting cities, that Nephites and Lamanites must take up arms together.
Converted Lamanites join the Nephites, forced to fight to protect their families, their rights, their church, their worship, and their freedom.
Before the year ends, the war is so severe that the Nephites face complete destruction.
The Lamanites who united with the Nephites are counted as Nephites, one people.

Their “curse” is lifted. In the Book of Mormon the curse was mainly being cut off from the Lord’s presence. Language about skin color here is hard for modern readers; the Church today rejects any idea that dark skin is a sign of God’s disfavor.

f.w: their curse was taken from them

f.g: Many readers note that “white” and “fair” in scripture often carry meanings of purity and being made clean.

chapters.n: Their young people became “exceedingly fair” and were called Nephites. The emphasis is that former divisions are erased: they are fully one people.
In the fourteenth year the war remains fierce, but the Nephites gain some advantage and drive the robbers back to the mountains and hideouts.
In the fifteenth year the robbers attack again and gain the upper hand because of the Nephites’ wickedness and internal quarrels.
The year ends with the people in great distress, the sword of destruction hanging over them because of their sins.

f.w: the sword of destruction did hang over them

chapters.n: In AD 16, Lachoneus, the Nephite governor, receives a letter from the leader of the Gadianton robbers.
Giddianhi opens with flattery, praising Lachoneus and his people for defending their liberty “as if” a god supported them, while sneering at what they “call” their rights.

f.w: or that which ye do call so
f.g: A sneer: he hints their claims to liberty and property are not real.

chapters.n: Then the threat: it is foolish to resist his many brave men, who are armed and eager for the order to destroy the Nephites.
He boasts that his warriors are unconquerable and filled with hatred for supposed wrongs the Nephites did them, and would destroy them completely.
He claims to write out of concern for Lachoneus’s welfare, admiring his courage, a mask of kindness over a threat.
His demand: surrender your cities, lands, and possessions to avoid the sword.
Or rather, join us: learn our secret works and become our “brethren and partners,” not slaves. The invitation is to share in the crimes and their profits.
He swears an oath: surrender and live, or in a month his armies will attack without mercy until the Nephites are extinct.

f.g: A month from now; next month.

chapters.n: He names himself: Giddianhi, governor of the secret society of Gadianton. He claims its works are good and ancient, handed down over generations.
He hopes for peaceful surrender so his people can “recover their rights.” He casts the dissenters as victims of Nephite injustice and threatens revenge.
Lachoneus is stunned by Giddianhi’s boldness. The so-called wronged dissenters had only wronged themselves by joining the robbers.
A just man, Lachoneus is not intimidated. He ignores the letter and calls his people to pray to the Lord for strength.

f.w: cry unto the Lord for strength

chapters.n: He orders everyone to gather their families, flocks, herds, and possessions into one place, leaving only the land itself. Robbers who live by plunder will find nothing to steal.
He has strong fortifications built around them, and Nephite and Lamanite soldiers guard them day and night.
Lachoneus insists that defenses alone are not enough: unless they repent and cry to the Lord, they will not be delivered.

f.g: A solemn oath affirming that what follows is certain.

chapters.n: His prophetic words fill the people with awe, and they work with all their might to follow his instructions.
Lachoneus appoints chief captains over all the armies.
The supreme commander is Gidgiddoni.
Mormon notes a Nephite custom: except in wicked times, chief captains were men with the spirit of revelation and prophecy. Gidgiddoni was a great prophet, and so was the chief judge.

f.w: spirit of revelation and also prophecy

chapters.n: The people want to go on the offensive: pray, then attack the robbers in their mountain strongholds.

Gidgiddoni refuses. If they attack, the Lord will give them into the robbers’ hands. Instead they will gather in the center of their lands and wait; then the Lord will deliver the robbers to them. A defensive war has God’s backing.

f.w: we will wait till they shall come against us

chapters.n: By late in AD 17 the gathering is complete. Thousands upon thousands march with horses, chariots, livestock, grain, and goods to the appointed place.

f.g: Wheeled vehicles or carts; the text gives no further detail.

chapters.n: The gathering place stretched from Zarahemla to the line between Bountiful and Desolation.
Many thousands gather. Lachoneus chose the southern land because of the great curse on the land northward.

f.w: the great curse which was upon the land northward

chapters.n: United and fortified, the people take Lachoneus’s words to heart. They repent of all their sins and pray for deliverance.
Though sorrowful about their enemies, they prepare, making all kinds of weapons and armor as Gidgiddoni directs. Faith and preparation work together.
Late in AD 18 the robbers pour out of their mountain hideouts and occupy the lands and cities the Nephites have abandoned, both north and south.
But the abandoned lands have no wild game; the only hunting is far off in the wilderness.
The robbers can only survive in the wilderness, because the Nephites took all their animals and goods with them. Lachoneus’s strategy is working.
Their only option is open battle. Meanwhile, the Nephites are united, numerous, and stocked with enough food and livestock for seven years.
In AD 19 Giddianhi realizes he must attack, because his people can only live by plunder and murder.
They don’t dare spread out to farm for fear of Nephite attack, so Giddianhi orders an assault.
They attack in the sixth month looking terrifying: lambskin loincloths, bodies dyed with blood, shaved heads, and helmets. The display was meant to frighten.

f.g: Dressed; with clothing belted around the waist.

chapters.n: Seeing them, the Nephite armies all fall to the ground and cry to the Lord to spare and deliver them.

f.w: did lift their cries to the Lord

chapters.n: Giddianhi’s men shout for joy, thinking the Nephites have collapsed in fear.
They are wrong. The Nephites fear God, not the robbers. Having prayed, they rise ready to meet the attack in the Lord’s strength.

f.w: in the strength of the Lord

chapters.n: The battle is terrible, the greatest slaughter among Lehi’s descendants since he left Jerusalem.
Despite Giddianhi’s threats and oaths, the Nephites beat the robbers back.
Gidgiddoni orders his army to pursue to the edge of the wilderness and not spare any they catch. They carry out his command.
Giddianhi fought boldly but, exhausted, he is caught and killed while fleeing. So ends the robber chief.
The Nephites return to their stronghold. The robbers don’t attack again for two years.
In AD 21 the robbers try a siege instead, surrounding the Nephites to cut them off and force surrender.

f.g: Surround a place to cut off supplies and force surrender.
Access to resources outside their stronghold.

chapters.n: Their new leader, Zemnarihah, orders the siege.

f.g: Giddianhi’s successor as leader of the robbers.

chapters.n: The siege actually helps the Nephites, because their stored provisions far outlast any siege.
The robbers, meanwhile, have only meat from hunting in the wilderness.
As wild game runs out, the robbers are close to starving.
The Nephites raid day and night, killing robbers by the thousands.
Zemnarihah’s people want to give up the siege because of their heavy losses.
Zemnarihah orders a retreat to the far reaches of the land northward.
Gidgiddoni, aware of their plan and their weakness, sends his armies by night to block the retreat route.
By morning the Nephites are ahead of them, so when the robbers march out, they are trapped front and rear.
Robbers in the south are also cut off. Mormon credits Gidgiddoni’s inspired leadership.
Many thousands surrender as prisoners; the rest are killed.
Zemnarihah is hanged from the top of a tree, and the tree is then cut down. The fallen tree becomes a symbol, and the people shout a prayer.
Their prayer: may the Lord keep His people righteous and pure, so that all who seek power through secret combinations will be cut down like this man.
They pray that the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob will protect them as long as they call on Him in righteousness. Protection is tied to continued faithfulness.

f.w: the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob

chapters.n: Everyone bursts into song, praising God for saving them.
They shout “Hosanna to the Most High God!” Hosanna is a Hebrew cry meaning “save, please,” which became a shout of praise.

f.g: Hebrew hoshiʿa-na, “save now, please”; used as an exclamation of praise.

chapters.n: Overflowing with joy and tears, they recognize that their repentance and humility, not just their strategy, saved them from destruction.

f.w: because of their repentance and their humility

chapters.n: After their deliverance, not one Nephite doubts the prophets anymore. They know every prophecy must be fulfilled.
The many signs prove that Christ has come, and what has already happened assures them that all remaining prophecies will come true too.
So they abandon their sins and serve God diligently day and night. Deliverance turns into devotion.

Every robber is either killed or captured. The prisoners hear God’s word preached to them, and those who repent and covenant to murder no more are set free. Mercy and gospel teaching come before punishment.

f.w: the word of God to be preached unto them

chapters.n: Those who refuse the covenant and still plot murder or threaten others are tried and punished under the law.
This ends the secret combinations that had caused so much wickedness and murder, at least for now.
Years twenty-two through twenty-five pass. A quarter-century has gone by since Christ’s birth.
Much more happened than could be written. Mormon says this book can’t hold even a hundredth of it.
Fuller records exist, and Nephi kept a shorter but true account.
Mormon bases his record on Nephi’s, engraved on what were called the plates of Nephi.
Mormon engraves his account on metal plates he made with his own hands. These are the plates later given to Joseph Smith.

f.w: plates which I have made with mine own hands

chapters.n: For the first time, the abridger introduces himself: he is Mormon, named after the land of Mormon, where Alma the Elder founded the church after King Noah’s wickedness.
His identity in one line: “a disciple of Jesus Christ,” called by Him to declare His word so people can have eternal life.
Mormon writes according to God’s will, so that the prayers of earlier holy prophets for their people’s record will be answered.

f.w: the prayers of those who have gone hence

chapters.n: His record is a short account covering from Lehi’s departure to Mormon’s own day.
He uses the records of earlier prophets for the time before his own life.
For his own era he writes what he witnessed personally.
He affirms the record is just and true, though their language limits what they can write.

f.w: according to our language, we are not able to write

chapters.n: Mormon ends his personal aside and returns to the history.
He is a “pure descendant of Lehi,” and he thanks God and Jesus Christ for secretly leading Lehi’s family out of Jerusalem and for giving his people so much saving knowledge.
God has blessed the house of Jacob and been merciful to Joseph’s descendants. Lehi was of the tribe of Joseph through Manasseh.
Whenever Lehi’s children kept God’s commandments, He blessed and prospered them as promised.

f.w: prospered them according to his word

chapters.n: God will surely bring a remnant of Joseph’s descendants back to knowledge of the Lord.

f.w: a remnant of the seed of Joseph

chapters.n: And He will gather the scattered remnants of Jacob from the four corners of the earth.

f.w: the four quarters of the earth

chapters.n: God made covenants with all of Jacob’s house, and in His own time He will fulfill them, restoring Israel to knowledge of those covenants.
Then they will know their Redeemer, Jesus Christ, and be gathered back to their lands. The gathering of Israel is ultimately a gathering to Christ.
In AD 26, with the robbers defeated, every family returns home with its animals and belongings.
Their seven-year supply was not used up, so they carry home the remaining grain, gold, silver, and valuables to lands north and south.
Former robbers who had covenanted to keep the peace, and who wanted to live as Lamanites, are given land to farm. Rehabilitation, not revenge, builds lasting peace.

f.w: entered into a covenant to keep the peace

chapters.n: The people prosper again. There is good order and laws based on fairness and justice.
Nothing could stop their prosperity except their own sin. The only real threat now comes from within.

f.w: except they should fall into transgression

chapters.n: Mormon credits Gidgiddoni, Lachoneus, and the other appointed leaders with establishing this peace.
Many new cities are built and old ones repaired.
Many highways and roads are built, connecting cities and lands.

f.g: Built up; raised, as a raised roadway.

chapters.n: The twenty-eighth year passes in continuous peace.
In the twenty-ninth year arguments begin. Some become proud and boastful because of great wealth, even persecuting others.
The economy now has many merchants, lawyers, and officials, new classes of people with money and influence.
Society splits into classes by wealth and education. The poor remain uneducated while the rich gain learning. Inequality feeds on itself.
Some grow proud, others humble. Some return insult for insult, while the humble endure abuse without retaliating and stay penitent before God.
This inequality breaks up the church throughout the land by AD 30, except among a few converted Lamanites who remain firm, steadfast, and immovable.
The cause: Satan’s great power, puffing people up with pride and tempting them to seek power, authority, riches, and worldly vanities.
So Satan leads their hearts astray, and their peace lasts only a few years.
By the start of AD 30, having let the devil lead them wherever he wished for a long time, the people are in a state of awful wickedness.
They did not sin out of ignorance. They knew God’s will and chose to rebel deliberately, which makes their sin more serious.
The governor is now Lachoneus, son of the Lachoneus who led the defense against the robbers.
Inspired men go out everywhere, boldly preaching against the people’s sins and testifying of Christ’s coming redemption, His death, sufferings, and resurrection.
Many become furious at these prophets, especially chief judges, former high priests, and lawyers. Those with power and status feel most threatened.
By law, no judge, lawyer, or high priest could sentence anyone to death without the governor’s signature.
Yet many bold witnesses for Christ are secretly executed by the judges, and the governor learns of it only afterward.
This was illegal: no one could be executed without the governor’s authority.
A complaint goes to the governor in Zarahemla against the judges who unlawfully condemned the Lord’s prophets.
The judges are arrested and brought to trial under the people’s law.
But the accused judges have many friends and relatives. Almost all the lawyers and high priests join with them.
They enter into the ancient covenant of secret combinations, originally given by the devil, uniting against all righteousness.

f.w: that covenant which was given by them of old

chapters.n: They conspire to destroy the Lord’s people and to rescue the murderers from justice.
They defy the law and the people’s rights, plotting to kill the governor and set up a king, ending the people’s liberty. It echoes the king-men of Captain Moroni’s day.

f.w: establish a king over the land

chapters.n: The conspirators never manage to crown a king over the whole land, but they do murder the chief judge on his judgment-seat that same year, AD 30.
The nation fractures. People separate into tribes based on family, relatives, and friends, and the central government collapses.

f.g: Groups organized by family and clan loyalty rather than by law.

chapters.n: Each tribe chooses its own chief or leader.
Since every leader had large extended families and many friends, the tribes become very large.
Surprisingly, there is no war yet. But all this wickedness came because they surrendered to Satan’s power.
The government’s structure is destroyed by the secret combination of the prophet-murderers’ friends and relatives.

f.g: The ordered systems and laws of government.

chapters.n: Contention spreads until even most of the formerly righteous become wicked. Only a few righteous people remain.
Not even six years have passed since their great deliverance, and most have returned to sin like a dog to its vomit or a pig to the mud. The vivid proverb shows how disgusting turning back is.

f.w: like the dog to his vomit

chapters.n: The secret combination gathers and places at its head a man named Jacob.

f.g: A leader of the secret band; not the brother of Nephi.

chapters.n: They call him their king. He was one of the leaders who had spoken out against the prophets who testified of Jesus.

f.w: given his voice against the prophets

chapters.n: The band is outnumbered by the tribes. Though the tribes aren’t righteous and each has its own laws, they share one thing: hatred of those who conspired to destroy the government.
Outnumbered, Jacob leads his followers to the far north to build a kingdom and wait for dissenters to join them, flattering them that many would. Indeed they do.
They move so fast no one can stop them. The thirtieth year ends.

In AD 31 the tribes agree not to war with each other and set strict rules against trespassing on one another, which keeps some peace. But their hearts have turned from God; they stone and expel the prophets.
Nephi, the record keeper, had been visited by angels and the Lord’s voice and knew Christ’s ministry. He had also witnessed how quickly the people turned back to wickedness.
Grieved by their hard hearts and blind minds, Nephi goes out and boldly preaches repentance and forgiveness through faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.
Nephi teaches with great power and authority. Mormon leaves most of it out because a partial account would not do it justice.
People are angry with him precisely because his power is greater than theirs. His faith is so great that angels minister to him daily, and his words are impossible to deny.

f.w: angels did minister unto him daily

chapters.n: In Jesus’s name he casts out devils and unclean spirits, and even raises his brother from the dead after the people stoned him. This is one of the few resurrection-type miracles in the Book of Mormon.

f.w: his brother did he raise from the dead

chapters.n: People witness these miracles but only grow angrier at his power. He performs many more miracles in Jesus’s name.
The thirty-first year ends with few converts. But those converted testify that God’s power and Spirit in Jesus Christ have touched them.
Those freed from evil spirits and healed of sickness testify that the Spirit of God worked on them, and some of them also perform signs and miracles.
The thirty-second year passes. At the start of the thirty-third, Nephi again preaches repentance and forgiveness.
Mormon emphasizes that everyone who repented was baptized with water. Baptism was not optional.
Nephi ordains men to baptize, so converts can be baptized as a witness before God and the people that they had repented and been forgiven.
Many are baptized early in AD 33, the year that will bring the great destruction and Christ’s appearance.
Mormon vouches for his source: the record keeper, Nephi, was a just man who worked miracles in Jesus’s name, something no one could do unless fully cleansed from sin.

f.w: a just man who did keep the record

chapters.n: If Nephi counted the years correctly (Mormon is careful and humble), the thirty-third year since the sign of Christ’s birth has passed.
People watch anxiously for Samuel’s second sign: three days of darkness at Christ’s death.

f.w: darkness for the space of three days

chapters.n: Despite all the signs already given, many doubt and argue.
On the fourth day of the first month of AD 34, an unprecedented storm arises. This lines up with Jesus’s crucifixion in Jerusalem.

f.g: Counting from the sign of Christ’s birth, matching the time of His death.

chapters.n: A terrible tempest comes, with thunder so violent it shakes the earth as though it would split apart.
Lightning more intense than anything ever seen strikes the land.
The capital city of Zarahemla catches fire.
The coastal city of Moroni sinks into the sea, and its people drown.
Earth is heaped over the city of Moronihah, leaving a mountain where it stood, as Samuel and Mormon had described.
The land southward suffers great destruction.
The land northward suffers even worse. Its whole face is changed by storms, whirlwinds, thunder, lightning, and massive earthquakes.
Highways break apart, level roads are ruined, and smooth ground becomes rough.
Many great cities sink, burn, or collapse in earthquakes, killing their inhabitants and leaving the places empty.
Some cities survive but suffer great damage and loss of life.
Some people are carried off by whirlwinds, and no one knows where they went.
The whole land is “deformed”: its shape and features permanently altered.
Rocks split everywhere and are left in fragments, seams, and cracks, exactly as Samuel prophesied.

f.w: the rocks were rent in twain

chapters.n: The violence lasts about three hours, though some thought longer. Then darkness falls. The three hours echo the three hours of darkness at the crucifixion.

f.w: about the space of three hours

chapters.n: The darkness is so thick that survivors can feel it as a vapor, like the darkness that fell on Egypt.
No light can be made at all. Candles, torches, and even very dry wood will not light.
No glimmer, fire, sun, moon, or stars can be seen through the mists of darkness.
The darkness lasts three days, matching Jesus’s time in the tomb. The people mourn, weep, and groan continually.

f.w: for the space of three days

chapters.n: Survivors cry out in regret: if only we had repented, our loved ones would not have burned in Zarahemla.

Others mourn: if only we had not killed, stoned, and expelled the prophets, our mothers, daughters, and children would not have been buried in Moronihah. Their words echo Samuel’s prophecy almost exactly.
In the darkness, a voice is heard throughout the land, by everyone at once.

The voice cries “Wo” three times: to this people and to the whole earth unless they repent. The devil and his angels rejoice over the dead, who fell because of their sins. The Lord does not delight in their destruction.

f.g: Old spelling of “woe”: grief or calamity.

chapters.n: The speaker takes responsibility: He burned the great city of Zarahemla and its inhabitants.
He sank the city of Moroni into the sea.
He buried Moronihah, hiding its wickedness from His sight so that the blood of murdered prophets would no longer cry out against them. This phrase repeats throughout the list.

f.w: the blood of the prophets and the saints

chapters.n: He sank the city of Gilgal and buried its people in the earth.

f.g: A Nephite city sharing its name with an important site in ancient Israel.

chapters.n: Onihah, Mocum, and a Nephite city called Jerusalem were covered by water to hide their wickedness.

f.g: A New World city named after the old, built by Lamanites and Amalekites.

chapters.n: Gadiandi, Gadiomnah, Jacob, and Gimgimno were sunk, with hills and valleys formed in their place.
Jacobugath, city of “king” Jacob’s people, was burned because its secret murders and combinations exceeded the wickedness of the whole earth. They had destroyed the peace and government of the land.
Laman, Josh, Gad, and Kishkumen were burned because they cast out and stoned the prophets God sent.

f.g: A city apparently named after the founder of the Gadianton band.

chapters.n: These cities had driven out every righteous person, leaving none to preserve them, so He sent fire. The pattern Samuel warned of came true.

f.w: there were none righteous among them
cry unto me from the ground

chapters.n: Many great destructions came on the land because of wickedness and abominations.
Then the tone shifts from judgment to invitation. To the survivors, spared because they were more righteous: won’t you return, repent, and be converted so I can heal you?
Whoever comes to Him will have eternal life. His “arm of mercy” is stretched out, and He will receive anyone who comes.

f.w: mine arm of mercy is extended towards you

chapters.n: The speaker identifies Himself: Jesus Christ, the Son of God, Creator of heaven and earth, one with the Father from the beginning, through whom the Father is glorified.

f.w: I am Jesus Christ the Son of God
I am in the Father, and the Father in me
I created the heavens and the earth

chapters.n: He came to His own people, and they rejected Him, fulfilling the scriptures about His coming.
To all who receive and believe on Him, He gives power to become sons and daughters of God. Redemption comes through Him, and the law of Moses is fulfilled in Him.

f.w: to become the sons of God
in me is the law of Moses fulfilled

chapters.n: He is the light and life of the world, Alpha and Omega, the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, meaning He is the beginning and the end.

f.w: the light and the life of the world

chapters.n: Animal sacrifices and burnt offerings are now done away, since they pointed to His sacrifice, which is complete.

f.w: your sacrifices and your burnt offerings shall be done away

chapters.n: The new sacrifice is a broken heart and a contrite spirit. Those who offer it, He will baptize with fire and the Holy Ghost, as happened to converted Lamanites who did not even realize it.

f.w: a broken heart and a contrite spirit
baptize with fire and with the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: He came to redeem the world and save it from sin.

f.w: to save the world from sin

chapters.n: Whoever repents and comes to Him as a little child, He will receive, for the kingdom of God belongs to such. For them He laid down His life and took it up again. He calls the ends of the earth to come and be saved.

f.w: laid down my life, and have taken it up again

chapters.n: Everyone in the land hears the voice. Afterward there is total silence for many hours.
The people are so astonished that they stop wailing for their dead. A stunned hush falls over the whole land.
Then the voice speaks again, and everyone hears it.
Christ addresses the people of the fallen cities as descendants of Jacob, the house of Israel. How often has He gathered and nourished them like a hen sheltering her chicks under her wings.

f.w: as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings

chapters.n: How often He would have gathered them, the fallen of Israel and those in Jerusalem alike, but they would not. He respects their agency even in His grief.
To the survivors He promises: He will gather them under His wings if they repent and return with full purpose of heart, sincerely and wholeheartedly.
If they refuse, their homes will lie desolate until the covenant made with their fathers is fulfilled, pointing to the latter-day gathering of Israel.
Hearing this, the people begin weeping and wailing again for their lost families and friends.
After three days the darkness lifts in the morning. The earthquakes, splitting rocks, groaning, and noise all stop. Light returns on the third day, as Christ rose on the third day.
The earth settles. The survivors’ mourning turns to joy, and their laments to praise and thanks to Jesus Christ, their Redeemer.

f.w: their mourning was turned into joy

chapters.n: So far, the prophets’ words have been fulfilled exactly.
Those spared were the more righteous: those who accepted the prophets rather than stoning them, and who had not shed the blood of the saints.

f.w: the more righteous part of the people

chapters.n: They escaped every form of destruction: sinking, drowning, fire, being crushed, whirlwinds, and suffocating smoke and darkness.
Mormon speaks directly to readers: whoever has the scriptures should search them and see that all these destructions fulfilled the prophecies of many holy prophets.
Many prophets testified of these events at Christ’s coming, and many were killed for it.
Zenos and Zenock, ancient Israelite prophets known from the brass plates, testified specifically about Lehi’s descendants, the remnant of their seed.
The patriarch Jacob also prophesied about a remnant of Joseph’s seed, which Mormon applies to his own people. These prophecies were on the brass plates Lehi brought.

f.w: a remnant of the seed of Joseph

chapters.n: Late in AD 34, the surviving Nephites and Lamanites receive great blessings: soon after His ascension, Christ truly shows Himself to them.

f.w: the ascension of Christ into heaven

chapters.n: He shows them His body and ministers to them. Mormon promises a full account next and ends his comments here.
A great crowd gathers around the temple in the land Bountiful, amazed at the dramatic changes in the land and pointing them out to each other.

f.w: the temple which was in the land Bountiful

chapters.n: They are also talking about Jesus Christ, whose death had been marked by the sign of darkness.
They hear a voice from heaven that is neither harsh nor loud, but small. Yet it pierces them to the core, makes their whole bodies tremble, and makes their hearts burn.

f.w: did cause their hearts to burn

chapters.n: They hear it a second time, but still don’t understand.
The third time, they open their ears, turn toward the sound, and gaze steadily toward heaven. Understanding comes when they give it their full attention.
This time they understand what the voice says.

God the Father introduces His Son: “Behold my Beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased... hear ye him.” Similar words are heard at Jesus’s baptism, on the Mount of Transfiguration, and in Joseph Smith’s First Vision.
Looking up, they see a Man in a white robe descend from heaven and stand among them. Silent and awestruck, they assume he is an angel.
He stretches out His hand and speaks.
“I am Jesus Christ, whom the prophets testified shall come.” Centuries of prophecy are fulfilled in a single sentence.

His first words describe His Atonement: He is the light and life of the world, has drunk the bitter cup the Father gave, and took on the sins of the world, submitting to the Father’s will in everything.

f.w: the light and the life of the world

chapters.n: The whole crowd falls to the ground, remembering the prophecy that Christ would show Himself to them after His ascension.
The Lord speaks to them.

He invites them to come and thrust their hands into His side and feel the nail prints in His hands and feet, so they will know He is the God of Israel and of the whole earth, slain for the world’s sins.

f.w: thrust your hands into my side

chapters.n: One by one, every person comes forward, sees and feels the wounds, and becomes a sure witness. Christ ministers to individuals, not just crowds. The record later counts about 2,500 people present.
When all have witnessed for themselves, they cry out together.
“Hosanna! Blessed be the name of the Most High God!” They fall at Jesus’s feet and worship Him.

f.g: Hebrew “save, we pray”; a shout of praise.

chapters.n: Jesus calls Nephi, the record keeper, forward from the crowd.
Nephi bows and kisses the Lord’s feet, a gesture of deep reverence and love.
The Lord tells him to stand, and he stands before Him.
Jesus gives Nephi authority to baptize the people after He ascends again.
He gives the same authority to others and teaches the exact way to baptize, so there will be no arguments over it.
Whoever repents and desires baptism in His name is to be baptized this way: the baptizer goes down and stands in the water.
These are the exact words to use, calling the person by name.
The baptismal prayer: by authority from Jesus Christ, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. Latter-day Saints use nearly the same words today.

f.w: Having authority given me of Jesus Christ

chapters.n: Then the person is immersed completely and brought out of the water, symbolizing burial and rebirth.
Baptism is done this way because the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are one, united in purpose. Christ is in the Father, and the Father in Him.

f.w: the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost are one

chapters.n: No more disputes about baptism or about His doctrine, as there had been before.
The spirit of contention comes not from Christ but from the devil, the “father of contention,” who stirs people to angry arguments.
Christ’s doctrine is not to stir up anger; it is that such anger should be done away with. How we discuss truth matters too.
He now declares His doctrine plainly.
His doctrine comes from the Father. The Father, Son, and Holy Ghost bear witness of each other. The Father commands everyone everywhere to repent and believe in Christ.

f.w: the Father beareth record of me

chapters.n: Whoever believes in Him and is baptized will be saved and inherit the kingdom of God.

f.w: whoso believeth in me, and is baptized

chapters.n: Whoever does not believe and is not baptized will be damned, meaning stopped in their progress and unable to enter God’s kingdom.

f.g: Condemned; stopped from progressing into God’s presence.

chapters.n: Whoever believes in Christ believes in the Father, and the Father will testify of Christ to that person by visiting them with fire and the Holy Ghost.

f.w: fire and with the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: The Father testifies of the Son, and the Holy Ghost testifies of both, because the three are one.

f.w: the Father, and I, and the Holy Ghost are one

chapters.n: They must repent, become as little children, and be baptized, or they cannot receive these things.
He repeats it for emphasis: repent, be baptized, become as a little child, or you cannot inherit God’s kingdom.

f.g: In no way; not at all.

chapters.n: Whoever builds on this doctrine builds on Christ’s rock, and the gates of hell will not prevail against them.

f.w: the gates of hell shall not prevail

chapters.n: Anyone who declares more or less than this as His doctrine builds on sand, and the gates of hell stand open to receive them when storms come. Christ guards the simplicity of His core message.
He sends them to declare His words to the people and to the ends of the earth.

f.w: unto the ends of the earth

chapters.n: Jesus has called twelve disciples with authority to baptize. He tells the crowd they are blessed if they follow these Twelve, are baptized by them with water, and then receive His baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost. Those who have seen Him and believe are blessed.

f.w: baptize you with fire and with the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: Even more blessed are those who believe without seeing, through the testimony of these witnesses, and humbly accept baptism. This blessing reaches all later believers, including us.

f.w: more blessed are they who shall believe in your words

chapters.n: The Beatitudes begin, much as in Matthew 5. Here Jesus adds “who come unto me”: being humble in spirit is the start, coming to Christ completes it. Such people receive the kingdom of heaven.

f.g: Humble, aware of one’s spiritual need.
Not in Matthew 5:3; the Book of Mormon ties the blessing to coming to Christ.

chapters.n: Those who mourn, whether for sin, loss, or suffering, will be comforted.
The meek, gentle and teachable rather than weak, will inherit the earth.
Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be filled. Here the Book of Mormon specifies: “filled with the Holy Ghost.”

f.g: Matthew 5:6 says only “filled”; this version names what fills them.

chapters.n: The merciful will receive mercy. How we treat others shapes how we are treated.
The pure in heart will see God, a promise fulfilled literally for this very crowd.
Peacemakers will be called God’s children because they act like Him.
Those persecuted for Christ’s sake will have the kingdom of heaven.

f.g: Matthew 5:10 says “for righteousness’ sake”; here the focus is on loyalty to Christ.

chapters.n: Blessed are those insulted, persecuted, and falsely accused because of Christ.
They should rejoice, because their heavenly reward will be great, and the prophets before them were treated the same way.
Jesus makes His disciples the salt of the earth. Salt that loses its flavor is useless and thrown out. Disciples must keep their distinct goodness to bless the world.
They are to be the light of this people, like a city on a hill that cannot be hidden.

f.w: A city that is set on a hill

chapters.n: No one lights a lamp and covers it with a basket; they set it on a stand to light the whole house.

f.g: A basket or container for measuring grain.

chapters.n: So let your light shine so that others see your good works and praise the Father, not you.
Jesus did not come to destroy the law or the prophets, but to fulfill them.

f.w: not come to destroy but to fulfil

chapters.n: Not the smallest detail of the law has been lost, but it has all been fulfilled in Him. This differs from Matthew, where fulfillment is still future; after the Resurrection, Christ speaks of it as complete.

f.w: in me it hath all been fulfilled

chapters.n: He has given them the Father’s commandments: believe in Him, repent, and come to Him with a broken heart and contrite spirit. The law is fulfilled, and these commandments now guide them.

f.w: a broken heart and a contrite spirit

chapters.n: So come to Him and be saved, but they must keep His present commandments to enter heaven. This replaces Matthew 5:19-20’s comparison with the scribes and Pharisees.

f.w: except ye shall keep my commandments

chapters.n: Jesus begins a series of contrasts. The old law said do not kill, and killers face judgment.

f.g: The ancients; earlier generations under the law of Moses.

chapters.n: But anger itself brings judgment. Contemptuous insults like “Raca” (empty-head) or “fool” bring greater danger still. Unlike most Bible manuscripts, this version omits “without a cause,” forbidding anger altogether.

f.g: An Aramaic insult meaning roughly “empty-headed” or “worthless.”
The local court or ruling body.
The Joseph Smith Translation of Matthew likewise drops “without a cause.”

chapters.n: If you come or want to come to Christ and remember someone has something against you...
...go and make peace first, then come to Him wholeheartedly, and He will receive you. In Matthew it’s bringing a gift to the altar; here, with sacrifices ended, it’s coming to Christ.

f.w: first be reconciled to thy brother

chapters.n: Settle disputes with your opponent quickly while you can, before it ends with you in prison.

f.g: Opponent, here in a legal dispute.

chapters.n: You won’t get out until you pay the last “senine,” the smallest Nephite coin. Jesus uses a local unit instead of the Roman farthing in Matthew. And in prison you can’t earn even one.

f.g: A Nephite measure of value, the smallest listed.

chapters.n: The old law said do not commit adultery.
But looking on someone with lust is already adultery in the heart. Christ’s law reaches thoughts, not just actions.

f.w: hath committed adultery already in his heart

chapters.n: Don’t let these things enter your heart at all. This replaces Matthew’s graphic image of plucking out an eye or cutting off a hand.

f.w: suffer none of these things to enter into your heart
f.g: Compare Matthew 5:29-30; the Book of Mormon states the principle directly.

chapters.n: It is better to deny yourself these things, taking up your cross, than to be cast into hell. Self-control is a form of discipleship.
The law allowed a man to divorce his wife by giving her a written certificate.
Jesus raises the standard: divorce except for sexual unfaithfulness leads to adultery, and so does marrying a divorced person. Marriage is meant to be lasting.

f.w: saving for the cause of fornication

chapters.n: The old law said not to break oaths made to the Lord.
Jesus says don’t swear oaths at all, not by heaven, which is God’s throne...
...nor by the earth, His footstool...
...nor by your own head, since you can’t even change the color of one hair.
Just let your “yes” mean yes and your “no” mean no. A truthful person needs no oaths.
The law said “an eye for an eye,” a principle that originally limited revenge to fair compensation.
But Jesus says don’t retaliate. If struck on the right cheek, an insulting backhand, turn the other. Answer insult with patience.

f.w: turn to him the other also

chapters.n: If someone sues for your coat, give your cloak too, going beyond what is demanded.

f.g: The outer garment, which under the law could not be kept overnight.

chapters.n: If forced to carry a load one mile, as Roman soldiers could require, go two. Generosity turns compulsion into service.
Give to those who ask, and don’t turn away those who want to borrow.

f.w: Give to him that asketh thee

chapters.n: It was said, love your neighbor and hate your enemy. (The law commands loving neighbors; hating enemies was a common attitude, not a written command.)
Jesus says: love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you.
This is how you become like your Father in heaven, who lets His sun rise on both the evil and the good.

f.w: he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good

chapters.n: The things of old under the law are all fulfilled in Him. This verse is unique to the Book of Mormon version.
Old things are done away, and all things have become new, a new covenant and a new way of life in Christ.
Be perfect, even as Christ or the Father is perfect. Unlike Matthew 5:48, the resurrected Jesus now includes Himself. “Perfect” suggests complete and whole, a goal reached through Christ.

f.g: Matthew mentions only the Father; now resurrected, Christ names Himself as perfected.

chapters.n: Jesus wants His people to give to the poor, but warns against giving to be seen. Seeking human praise forfeits the Father’s reward.
Don’t blow a trumpet when you give, as hypocrites do in public places to win admiration. The applause they get is their only reward.

f.g: From Greek for “stage actor”: someone performing a role.
They are paid in full already; nothing more is coming.

chapters.n: Give so quietly that even your left hand doesn’t know what your right is doing, a vivid picture of not keeping score.
Give in secret, and your Father, who sees what is hidden, will reward you openly.

f.w: thy Father who seeth in secret

chapters.n: Don’t pray like hypocrites who stand in public places to be seen praying.

f.g: Busy intersections where many would notice.

chapters.n: Instead, go into a private room, shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret. He will reward you openly.
Don’t use empty, mechanical repetitions like those who think more words get more attention.

f.g: Empty, thoughtless phrases repeated without meaning.
Those who did not know the true God.

chapters.n: Your Father already knows what you need before you ask. Prayer is about relationship, not informing God.
The Lord’s Prayer begins: “Our Father who art in heaven,” and His name is to be treated as holy. This is a pattern, “after this manner,” not a script.
May God’s will be done on earth as in heaven. Notably, this version omits “Thy kingdom come,” perhaps because the King Himself is present with them.

f.g: Matthew 6:10 also has “Thy kingdom come”; it is absent here.

chapters.n: Forgive us our debts as we forgive others. This version also leaves out the request for daily bread; some suggest it is because the Twelve are about to be told the Father will provide.

f.g: A Jewish way of speaking of sins as debts owed to God.
Matthew 6:11 “Give us this day our daily bread” is not in this version.

chapters.n: Don’t lead us into temptation, but rescue us from evil. The Joseph Smith Translation reads “suffer us not to be led into temptation.”
The prayer closes by giving God the kingdom, power, and glory forever. Amen.
Jesus explains one line: if you forgive others, the Father forgives you.
If you won’t forgive, your Father won’t forgive you. Forgiving others is part of receiving forgiveness.
When fasting, don’t look gloomy and messy to show off your devotion, like hypocrites do. That attention is their only reward.

f.g: Make unsightly; here, deliberately looking unkempt.

chapters.n: Instead, groom yourself normally, oil your hair and wash your face, so no one can tell.

f.g: Put oil on the hair, part of ordinary daily grooming then.

chapters.n: Fast for the Father, who sees in secret, and He will reward you openly.
Don’t store up treasures on earth, where moths, rust, and thieves can destroy or take them.

f.g: Moths ruined fine clothing, a common form of wealth then.

chapters.n: Store up treasures in heaven, which nothing can ruin or steal.
Your heart follows your treasure. What you value most shapes who you become.
The eye is the body’s lamp. If your eye is “single,” focused wholly on God, your whole self fills with light.
If your eye is evil, greedy or divided, your whole self is darkened. When the light within is actually darkness, the darkness is profound.

f.g: In Hebrew idiom, an “evil eye” often means stinginess or greed.

chapters.n: No one can serve two masters. You cannot serve God and Mammon, wealth treated as a god.

f.g: An Aramaic word for wealth or riches, pictured here as a rival master.

chapters.n: Jesus turns to His twelve chosen disciples. As full-time ministers, they should not worry about food, drink, or clothing. In the Book of Mormon, this counsel is directed specifically to the Twelve.

f.g: Matthew 6:25 addresses a general audience; here Jesus speaks to His ministers.

chapters.n: Look at the birds. They don’t plant, harvest, or store in barns, yet the Father feeds them. Aren’t you worth much more?
Can worrying add a single cubit, about a foot and a half, to your height? Anxiety changes nothing.

f.g: About 18 inches; the length of a forearm.
Height, or possibly length of life.

chapters.n: Why worry about clothing? Consider the wildflowers: they don’t work or spin thread.
Yet even King Solomon in all his splendor wasn’t dressed as beautifully as one of them.
If God clothes wild grass that is burned for fuel the next day, He will surely clothe you, unless your faith is small.
So don’t fret over what to eat, drink, or wear.
Your Father in heaven knows you need these things.
Put God’s kingdom and righteousness first, and everything else will be given to you as well. Priorities matter.

f.w: seek ye first the kingdom of God

chapters.n: Don’t worry about tomorrow; tomorrow will take care of itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.

f.w: Sufficient is the day unto the evil thereof
f.g: Each day has enough difficulty of its own; don’t borrow tomorrow’s.

chapters.n: Having spoken to the Twelve, Jesus turns back to the multitude: “Judge not, that ye be not judged.” He warns against harsh, hypocritical condemnation, not against all discernment.
The standard you use to judge others will be used on you. Generosity invites generosity.

f.g: Measure out; give out by measure.

chapters.n: Why focus on a speck of dust in your brother’s eye while ignoring the wooden beam in your own? The exaggeration is meant to be humorous and memorable.

f.g: A large wooden plank or rafter.

chapters.n: How can you offer to remove his speck when a beam is sticking out of your own eye?
Hypocrite: deal with your own faults first, and then you’ll see clearly enough to help your brother. Helping others is good, but it begins with self-examination.

Don’t give sacred things to those who will treat them with contempt, like throwing pearls to pigs, which will trample them and then turn on you. Sacred truths require wisdom about when and with whom to share them.
Ask, seek, knock: God answers persistent, sincere seekers. The verbs suggest ongoing action.

f.w: Ask, and it shall be given unto you

chapters.n: Everyone who asks receives, every seeker finds, every knocker has the door opened.
What father would give his son a stone when he asked for bread?
Or a snake when he asked for a fish?
If imperfect human parents know how to give good gifts, how much more will the perfect Father in heaven give good things to those who ask.
The Golden Rule: treat others the way you want to be treated. This sums up the law and the prophets.

f.w: this is the law and the prophets

chapters.n: Enter through the narrow gate. The wide gate and broad road lead to destruction, and many take it.
The gate to life is narrow and the road hard, and few find it. The image matches Nephi’s teaching of the gate of repentance and baptism and the strait and narrow path.
Beware of false prophets who look gentle as sheep but inside are ravenous wolves.
You can recognize them by their fruits, the results of their lives and teachings. Grapes don’t grow on thornbushes or figs on thistles.
Good trees produce good fruit; rotten trees produce bad fruit.
A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a rotten tree cannot bear good fruit. Character shows in results.
Trees that don’t bear good fruit are cut down and burned, a warning of judgment.

f.w: hewn down, and cast into the fire

chapters.n: So, by their fruits you will know them.
Not everyone who calls Jesus “Lord, Lord” will enter heaven, only those who do the Father’s will. Words of devotion must be matched by obedience.
On judgment day, many will point to their prophesying, casting out devils, and miracles in His name.
He will tell them, “I never knew you; depart from me.” The issue is relationship and righteous living, not public religious acts. The Joseph Smith Translation reads “Ye never knew me.”
Whoever hears His words and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on rock.

f.w: built his house upon a rock

chapters.n: Rain, floods, and wind beat on the house, but it stands because its foundation is rock. The storms come to everyone; the foundation decides the outcome.
Whoever hears but doesn’t obey is like a foolish man who built on sand.

f.w: built his house upon the sand

chapters.n: The same storms strike, and the house collapses with a great crash. The sermon ends with a choice: hearing must become doing.

f.w: great was the fall of it

chapters.n: Jesus tells the crowd they have heard what He taught before ascending to the Father, the Sermon on the Mount. Whoever remembers and lives these teachings He will raise up at the last day.

f.w: him will I raise up at the last day

chapters.n: He senses that some are puzzled about the law of Moses. They don’t understand how “old things” could have passed away and “all things” become new.
He tells them not to be surprised by that statement.
The law given to Moses is now fulfilled.
A remarkable claim: Jesus is the one who gave the law and made the covenant with Israel. As Jehovah, He gave it; as Christ, He fulfills it, so it has reached its end.

f.w: I am he that gave the law

chapters.n: He does not cancel the prophets. Any prophecies not yet fulfilled will still be fulfilled.

f.w: I do not destroy the prophets

chapters.n: Saying “old things have passed away” doesn’t erase prophecies about the future.
The covenant with Israel is not yet complete, but the law of Moses ends in Him. Christ separates the temporary law from the eternal covenant.

f.w: the covenant which I have made with my people is not all fulfilled

chapters.n: “I am the law, and the light.” Look to Him and endure to the end to receive eternal life. Christ Himself replaces the law as the standard.
He has given them commandments to keep. This is what the law and the prophets truly pointed to: they testified of Him.
Then Jesus speaks specifically to His twelve chosen disciples.
They are His disciples and a light to their people, who are a remnant of the house of Joseph.

f.w: a remnant of the house of Joseph

chapters.n: This land is their inheritance, given by the Father.
The Father never told Jesus to tell His followers in Jerusalem about the Nephites.
Nor to tell them about the other tribes of Israel the Father had led away.

f.g: The “lost” tribes of Israel, carried off by Assyria and scattered.

chapters.n: He was commanded to tell them only this much.
He quotes His own words from John 10: He has other sheep, not of this fold, who will hear His voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd.

f.w: other sheep I have which are not of this fold

chapters.n: Because of stubbornness and unbelief, His hearers in Jerusalem didn’t understand, so He was told to say no more about it.
The Father had Him reveal to the Nephites that they were separated from the Jews because of the Jews’ wickedness, which is why the Jews know nothing of them.
The other tribes were separated for the same reason, so they too are unknown.
Jesus now identifies the Nephites as the “other sheep” He spoke of at Jerusalem. The Book of Mormon claims to fulfill a New Testament saying.

f.w: ye are they of whom I said

chapters.n: His disciples in Jerusalem thought He meant the Gentiles. They didn’t understand that the Gentiles would be converted through the apostles’ preaching, not by His personal visit.

f.w: they supposed it had been the Gentiles

chapters.n: They missed that the “other sheep” would hear His voice in person, while the Gentiles would only know Him through the Holy Ghost.

f.w: save it were by the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: But the Nephites have both heard His voice and seen Him. They are His sheep, among those the Father gave Him.
Jesus reveals that He has still other sheep, not in this land or in Jerusalem or the areas around it where He ministered.
These people have not yet heard His voice or seen Him.

The Father has commanded Him to go to them so they too will hear His voice and join the one fold under one shepherd. So He will go and show Himself to them. Latter-day Saints understand this to include the lost tribes of Israel.

f.w: I go to show myself unto them

chapters.n: He commands the disciples to write these sayings. If His followers in Jerusalem don’t seek this knowledge by the Holy Ghost, these records will be preserved and come to the Gentiles, and through them the scattered descendants of Israel will be brought to know their Redeemer.
Then He will gather Israel from the four corners of the earth and fulfill the Father’s covenant with them.

f.w: gather them in from the four quarters of the earth

chapters.n: The Gentiles are blessed for believing in Him through the Holy Ghost, who testifies of Christ and the Father.

Because of Gentile belief and Israel’s unbelief, the fulness of the gospel will come to the Gentiles in the last days. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the Restoration and the coming forth of the Book of Mormon.

f.w: in the latter day shall the truth come unto the Gentiles

chapters.n: But woe to unbelieving Gentiles. They will come to this land, scatter the house of Israel, drive them out, and trample them, a prophecy many see fulfilled in the treatment of Native peoples of the Americas.
Through the Father’s mercy to the Gentiles and His judgments on Israel, Israel will be struck, afflicted, killed, expelled, hated, and mocked.

f.g: An object of scorn and a proverb of contempt.

chapters.n: The Father’s warning: when the Gentiles reject the fulness of His gospel and become proud above all nations, full of lies, deceit, hypocrisy, murder, priestcraft, immorality, and secret abominations, He will take the fulness of the gospel from them.

f.g: Preaching for money or praise rather than for God.

chapters.n: Then He will remember His covenant with Israel and bring the gospel to them.
The Gentiles will not have power over Israel, and Israel will come to know the fulness of the gospel.
But if the Gentiles repent and return, they will be counted among the Lord’s people Israel. Covenant belonging is open to all who repent.
Then He will not allow Israel to tread them down.
If they refuse, He will let Israel pass through and trample them. They will become like salt that has lost its flavor, fit only to be thrown out.

f.w: as salt that hath lost its savor

chapters.n: The Father has commanded that this land be given to Lehi’s people as their inheritance.
Then Isaiah’s words will be fulfilled. Jesus now quotes Isaiah 52:8-10, which He will return to in later chapters.
Zion’s watchmen, the prophets who watch over God’s people, will raise their voices and sing together. They will “see eye to eye,” face to face and in full agreement, when the Lord brings Zion back.

f.w: Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice

f.g: See directly and clearly; also, be united in understanding.

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s ruins are told to burst into song, because the Lord has comforted and redeemed His people. The wording matches the KJV of Isaiah 52:9.
The Lord has “made bare His holy arm,” like a warrior rolling up his sleeve to act. All nations will see God’s salvation, an image fulfilled in Christ and in the latter-day gathering.
Jesus has finished his first long sermon at the temple in Bountiful. Looking over the crowd, he signals that his time with them this day is almost over.

f.g: His time to leave for now has come; he will return the next day (verse 3).

chapters.n: Jesus gently admits that the people are not yet able to take in everything the Father has asked him to teach. He does not blame them; he simply sees their limits and plans around them.

f.g: Here “weak” means not yet ready to grasp it all, not sinful.

chapters.n: His solution is a pattern for any learner: go home, ponder, pray to the Father in Christ’s name for understanding, and prepare your mind for more. Revelation often comes after we think and ask.

f.g: To think carefully and turn something over in the mind.

f.w: ask of the Father, in my name

chapters.n: Jesus explains that he must return to the Father and also visit the scattered tribes of Israel. Those tribes are “lost” only to us; God knows exactly where they are.

f.g: The ten northern tribes carried away by Assyria about 722 BC.

chapters.n: The people are in tears and look at him intently, silently hoping he will stay a little longer. Their longing moves him to change his plans.
Jesus tells them his heart is overflowing with compassion for them. Christ is not a distant teacher here; he is deeply moved by their feelings.

f.g: In scriptural idiom the inner organs stand for the seat of deep feeling — “my heart is full of compassion.”

chapters.n: He invites them to bring every kind of sick and afflicted person to him for healing. His list is sweeping, so no one is left out.

f.g: Having a serious skin disease that made people outcasts in the ancient world.

chapters.n: Jesus senses that they long to see the miracles he did in Jerusalem, and that their faith is now strong enough for him to heal them. Faith precedes the miracle.
Everyone brings their sick together, and Jesus heals every single person. The phrase “every one” emphasizes that his power and love reach each individual.
Healed and healthy alike bow and worship him. Many kiss his feet and wet them with tears, echoing the woman who washed Jesus’ feet in Luke.

f.w: bathe his feet with their tears

chapters.n: Jesus now asks that the little children be brought to him. The focus shifts from the sick to the smallest and most innocent.
The children are seated in a circle around him on the ground while the crowd makes room. Jesus stands at the center of the little ones.
With the children gathered, Jesus asks the whole multitude to kneel. The setting becomes a moment of worship and prayer.
Jesus groans inwardly and tells the Father he is troubled by the wickedness of the house of Israel. Even in this joyful scene he carries sorrow for those who reject God.

f.g: A deep inner sigh of grief.

chapters.n: Jesus himself kneels and prays. What he says is so sacred that it cannot be written, yet everyone who heard it testifies of it.
The witnesses describe the prayer by saying no eye or ear had ever experienced anything so great. Their wording echoes Isaiah and Paul on the unseen glories God prepares.

f.w: The eye hath never seen, neither hath the ear heard

chapters.n: They continue: no tongue can tell it and no heart can imagine it. Most touching of all, he was praying for them, and that filled them with joy beyond words.

f.w: pray for us unto the Father

chapters.n: When Jesus stands up after praying, the people are so full of joy they are physically overcome and cannot rise.

f.g: Overwhelmed — unable to stand because of the intensity of the experience.

chapters.n: Jesus speaks to them and tells them to get up. Having lifted them spiritually, he now helps them stand.
He blesses them for their faith and declares that his own joy is now full. Their faith is not only good for them; it brings joy to the Savior.
Jesus weeps, then blesses each child one at a time and prays for them. “One by one” shows his personal, unhurried love for every child.
After blessing the children he weeps again. These seem to be tears of tender joy and love rather than sorrow.
He calls the multitude’s attention to their children: “Behold your little ones.” It is an invitation to see their children as heaven sees them.
Looking up, the people see heaven open and angels come down as if in fire. The angels surround the children with fire and minister to them — a sign of purity and divine protection.
Mormon stresses that about 2,500 men, women, and children were witnesses, each seeing and hearing for himself. This is a large, personal, and multiple witness of the risen Christ.

f.w: two thousand and five hundred souls
f.g: The number of eyewitnesses on this first day; the crowd grows much larger the next day (3 Nephi 19:2-5).

chapters.n: Jesus asks his twelve disciples to bring bread and wine. He is about to introduce the sacrament among the Nephites, just as he did with his apostles at the Last Supper.
While the disciples fetch the bread and wine, Jesus has the crowd sit down on the ground. The setting is calm and orderly, ready for a sacred ordinance.
Jesus breaks the bread, blesses it, and gives it first to the twelve. They are being shown how to perform the ordinance themselves.
After the disciples eat and are filled, Jesus tells them to pass the bread to the multitude. Those who receive the ordinance now serve others with it.

Jesus announces that one will be ordained with power to bless and pass the bread to the church — to those who believe and are baptized. The sacrament requires proper authority and is for baptized members.
This is to be a lasting practice, done exactly as he did it. The sacrament is not a one-time event but an ongoing ordinance of the church.
The bread is a reminder of the body they have seen and touched. Partaking witnesses to the Father that we always remember Christ, and the promise is that his Spirit will be with us.

f.w: ye shall have my Spirit to be with you

chapters.n: Next Jesus has the disciples drink from the cup of wine and then share it with the multitude. The pattern of blessing the bread is repeated with the cup.

f.g: Latter-day Saints today use water, as permitted in D&C 27:2.

chapters.n: The disciples drink and are filled, then serve the multitude, who are also filled. “Filled” hints at spiritual as well as physical satisfaction.
Jesus praises the disciples for doing what he commanded. Taking the sacrament shows the Father our willingness to obey — the same covenant language later used in the sacrament prayers.

f.w: willing to do that which I have commanded you

chapters.n: The wine is in remembrance of the blood he shed for them. The same promise is repeated: remember him always, and his Spirit will be with you.
Doing these things faithfully means being built on Christ’s rock — a sure foundation. His rock is his doctrine and gospel.
Anyone who adds to or takes away from these ordinances builds on sand and will fall when storms come. The image recalls Jesus’ parable of the wise and foolish builders.

f.w: do more or less than these

chapters.n: Jesus repeats that the blessing comes from keeping the commandments the Father gave him to deliver. He presents himself as carrying out the Father’s will.
He warns the disciples to watch and pray always so the devil cannot tempt them and lead them away as captives. Constant prayer is protection.
The disciples are to pray in the church just as Jesus has prayed among them. He is the light and the example to follow.
Having taught the twelve, Jesus turns back to the whole multitude to teach them as well.
He gives everyone the same warning to watch and pray. Satan wants to “sift” them like wheat — shaking them until the good is separated and lost.

f.g: Grain was shaken in a sieve; Satan wants to shake people loose from their faith.

chapters.n: So they must always pray to the Father in Christ’s name. This is the pattern of Christian prayer: to the Father, through the Son.

f.w: pray unto the Father in my name

chapters.n: A promise: whatever we ask in Christ’s name that is right, with faith that we will receive, will be given. The words “which is right” keep our requests aligned with God’s will.
Jesus commands family prayer, always in his name, so that spouses and children may be blessed. Prayer is to be part of home life, not only church life.
Believers should meet together often and never shut anyone out of their meetings. The church is to be open and welcoming.
Instead of casting people out, the church should pray for them — especially those who keep coming. Patience and prayer replace rejection.
“Hold up your light” means let your example shine. The light they hold up is Christ himself — doing what they have seen him do, such as praying to the Father.
Just as Jesus invited everyone to come close, feel, and see, his followers must invite the whole world to come to him. Refusing to do so leads a person into temptation.

f.w: that ye might feel and see

chapters.n: Jesus turns his attention back to the twelve disciples he has chosen for more specific instructions.
He has one more commandment for them before he must go to the Father to carry out other duties the Father has given him.
The disciples must not knowingly let anyone take the sacrament unworthily when they administer it. Leaders have a duty to protect the sacredness of the ordinance.

f.g: Without repentance or sincere intent to keep the covenant.

chapters.n: Partaking unworthily brings condemnation on one’s soul. So if they know someone is unworthy, they should stop him from partaking — for his own good.

f.g: Condemnation; being stopped in spiritual progress.

chapters.n: Yet such a person is not to be pushed away. They should minister to him and pray for him, and when he repents and is baptized, welcome him to the sacrament.
If he will not repent he is not counted among Christ’s people, so that he cannot harm the flock. Jesus, the Good Shepherd, knows and counts each of his sheep.
Even so, the unrepentant are not to be barred from worship services. No one knows who may yet return with full purpose of heart and be healed — and members may help bring that salvation.
Keeping these instructions keeps the disciples out of condemnation. Being condemned by the Father is a solemn thing.
Jesus explains that he gave these rules because there had been arguments among them. Peace and unity are themselves a blessing.
He now must go to the Father, and he says it is “expedient” — helpful and necessary — for their sake.
Jesus touches each of the twelve, one by one, speaking to each. This is the laying on of hands to give them authority.
The crowd could not hear what he said, but the disciples testified he gave them power to bestow the Holy Ghost. Mormon promises to prove this record true later.

f.w: power to give the Holy Ghost
I will show unto you hereafter

chapters.n: A cloud overshadows the crowd so that they can no longer see Jesus, as at his ascension in Jerusalem.
Hidden by the cloud, Jesus ascends to heaven. The disciples saw it and testified, closing the first day of his visit.
After Jesus ascends, the crowd breaks up and families go home together. The first day of his visit ends with ordinary people returning to ordinary homes, changed.
News spreads quickly, even before nightfall: Jesus had appeared, ministered to them, and would come again the next day.

f.g: Spread around by word of mouth.

chapters.n: All night the word goes out, and huge numbers of people work hard through the night to reach the place where Jesus will appear. Their effort shows how much they want to see him.
Mormon lists the twelve disciples Jesus chose, led by Nephi (son of Nephi), whose brother Timothy had been raised from the dead. They stand in the middle of the gathered crowd.

f.w: these were the names of the disciples

chapters.n: The crowd is so large that it is divided into twelve groups, one for each disciple to teach.
Each disciple teaches his group and has them kneel and pray to the Father in Jesus’ name, following the pattern Jesus taught the day before.

f.w: pray unto the Father in the name of Jesus

chapters.n: The disciples themselves also pray in Jesus’ name, then rise to serve and teach the people.
They repeat Jesus’ words exactly, without changing anything, and then kneel to pray again. Faithful teaching passes on the Lord’s message unaltered.
Their deepest desire, and the focus of their prayer, is to receive the Holy Ghost. This shows what truly matters most to them.
After praying, the disciples walk down to the water’s edge with the multitude following them.
Nephi goes down into the water and is baptized. He had been baptized before, but now is baptized again into the church Jesus has newly established among them.

f.g: Jesus had just given renewed authority and instructions for baptism.

chapters.n: Coming up from the water, Nephi then baptizes the other eleven chosen disciples.
Once all are baptized, the Holy Ghost falls on them and they are filled with the Holy Ghost and with fire, fulfilling Jesus’ promise.

f.w: with the Holy Ghost and with fire

chapters.n: They are visibly encircled by fire from heaven, witnessed by the crowd, and angels come to minister to them — just as angels had ministered to the children the day before.

f.w: encircled about as if it were by fire

chapters.n: While angels are ministering, Jesus himself appears and stands among them, serving the disciples personally.
Jesus has the multitude and the disciples kneel down on the earth again, preparing them for prayer.
With everyone kneeling, Jesus asks his disciples to pray.
The disciples pray to Jesus, calling him their Lord and their God. Normally prayer goes to the Father, but here Jesus is present in person, and they address him directly.

f.g: Jesus explains in verse 22 that they pray to him because he is with them.

chapters.n: Jesus withdraws a short distance, bows to the earth, and begins to pray, as he did in Gethsemane.
He thanks the Father for giving the Holy Ghost to his chosen disciples, explaining he chose them because they believed in him.

f.w: chosen them out of the world

chapters.n: Jesus prays that everyone who believes the disciples’ words will also receive the Holy Ghost. His concern reaches far beyond those present.

f.w: all them that shall believe in their words

chapters.n: He explains to the Father that the disciples pray to him because he is with them, and their prayers show their belief. Their faith in him is why they received the Spirit.
Jesus prays that all believers may be one with him as he is one with the Father. This oneness is unity of heart, purpose, and love.
Returning, Jesus finds the disciples still praying. They use few words, because the Spirit tells them what to pray, and they are full of holy desire.

f.g: Pile up words or repeat phrases.

f.w: it was given unto them what they should pray

chapters.n: Jesus smiles on them, and the light of his face shines upon them until they become as white as he is — whiter than anything on earth. This is a visible sign of their purity and his glory resting on them.
Jesus tells them to keep praying, and they do so without stopping. Prayer here is continuous communion, not a single request.
Again Jesus withdraws a little way, bows to the earth, and prays to the Father.
He thanks the Father for purifying the disciples because of their faith, and asks the same for all who believe their words. Purity comes “in me” — through Christ.

Echoing his Jerusalem prayer, Jesus prays not for the world in general but for those given him out of the world, that they may be purified, united with him and the Father, and that he may be glorified in them.

f.w: I pray not for the world
that I may be glorified in them

chapters.n: Returning again, Jesus finds them still praying steadily. He smiles on them once more, and they are white like him.
For a third time Jesus goes a short distance away and prays to the Father.
The words of this prayer are beyond human speech or writing. Like Paul’s experience, some sacred things cannot be put into words.
The multitude heard it and testify. Their hearts were opened so that they understood the prayer inwardly, by the Spirit, even though they cannot repeat it.
Mormon repeats the point: the prayer was so great and marvelous that it can neither be written nor spoken by man.
Jesus tells the disciples he never saw such great faith among the Jews, so he could not show them such great miracles because of their unbelief. Miracles follow faith.

f.w: So great faith have I never seen

chapters.n: None of the Jews had seen or heard such great things as these people. Their extraordinary experience is a fruit of their extraordinary faith.

f.w: none of them that have seen so great things
