chapters.n: Jesus asks everyone to stop praying aloud but to keep praying in their hearts. Prayer can continue silently as an attitude of the heart.
He has them stand up, and they rise to their feet, ready for what comes next.
Jesus again breaks and blesses bread and gives it to the disciples. This is the second time he administers the sacrament among them.
After eating, the disciples break bread and give it to the multitude, as they had been taught.
Then Jesus gives them wine to drink and has them share it with the multitude.
Mormon points out a remarkable detail: no one had brought any bread or wine this time.
Jesus truly provided the bread and wine miraculously, recalling his feeding of the multitudes in Galilee.

f.w: he truly gave unto them bread

chapters.n: Partaking nourishes the soul with his body and blood, and such a soul will never hunger or thirst but will be filled. The language echoes his “bread of life” teaching.
After the sacrament the people are filled with the Spirit and with one voice give glory to Jesus, whom they see and hear in person.
Jesus now completes the Father’s commandment concerning these people, whom he calls a remnant of the house of Israel. A long teaching on covenant and gathering begins.

f.w: remnant of the house of Israel
f.g: Lehi’s descendants are a surviving branch of the family of Israel (Jacob).

chapters.n: He reminds them that Isaiah’s words are written and in their hands, and tells them to search them. Isaiah is the key text for understanding the covenant.
When Isaiah’s prophecies are fulfilled, so is the Father’s covenant with Israel. Fulfilled prophecy and fulfilled covenant go together.
The scattered remnants of Israel will be gathered from every direction and brought to know the Lord their Redeemer. Gathering is both physical and spiritual — coming home to God.

f.w: gathered in from the east and from the west

chapters.n: The Father commands Jesus to give the Americas to Lehi’s descendants as their land of inheritance.
Jesus speaks of the latter-day Gentiles, who will be blessed yet will also scatter his people. If they do not repent after receiving such blessings, judgment will follow.

f.w: if the Gentiles do not repent

chapters.n: Then the remnant of Jacob will be among the unrepentant Gentiles like a young lion among sheep — unstoppable. Jesus is quoting the prophet Micah.

f.w: as a lion among the beasts of the forest

chapters.n: Continuing Micah, the remnant’s hand will be lifted against its enemies, and they will be cut off. The emphasis is that God will vindicate his covenant people.

f.w: Thy hand shall be lifted up

chapters.n: God will gather his people like a farmer gathering sheaves of grain onto the threshing floor. Harvest is a common image for the last days.

f.g: Bundles of cut grain brought to the threshing floor.

chapters.n: Quoting Micah again, God will make his people strong as an ox with iron horn and brass hoofs, and their gains will be dedicated to the Lord. Jesus declares, “I am he who doeth it.”

f.w: I will make thy horn iron
f.g: Horns symbolized strength; iron and brass suggest invincible power.

chapters.n: The Father warns that the sword of his justice will hang over the Gentile nations; unless they repent, it will fall on them.
God promises to establish his people, the house of Israel. Despite scattering, he will not forget them.
In this land God will establish his people and build a New Jerusalem, fulfilling his covenant with Jacob. The powers of heaven — and Christ himself — will be in their midst.

f.r: 3 Nephi 21:23-24; Ether 13:3-8; Articles of Faith 1:10; D&C 84:2-4

f.w: I will be in the midst of you

chapters.n: Jesus identifies himself as the prophet Moses foretold — one like Moses whom all must hear. Those who refuse to hear him cut themselves off.

f.w: A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up

chapters.n: All the prophets from Samuel onward testified of Christ. The whole prophetic tradition points to him.
Jesus tells the people they are children of the prophets and of the covenant God made with Abraham — that through his seed all the earth would be blessed.

f.w: in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed

chapters.n: Because they are covenant children, the Father sent Jesus to them first, to bless them by turning each person away from sin.

f.w: turning away every one of you from his iniquities

chapters.n: After blessing Israel, the Father extends Abraham’s covenant to the Gentiles by pouring out the Holy Ghost on them. That blessing makes the Gentiles mighty — though it will also coincide with the scattering of Israel.

f.w: pouring out of the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: The Gentiles will be a scourge — a punishment — to Lehi’s descendants. Yet if the Gentiles reject the fulness of the gospel after receiving it, their own sins will come back on them.
The Father will remember his covenant and, in his own time, gather the Jews and restore to them the land of Jerusalem as their eternal inheritance.
The time will come when the fulness of the gospel is preached to the Jews.
They will believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and pray to the Father in his name. Conversion to Christ is the heart of their gathering.
Jesus now quotes Isaiah 52: their watchmen will lift their voices and sing together, for they will “see eye to eye” — share a clear, united understanding.

f.w: their watchmen lift up their voice

f.g: Here probably “see face to face” or with full clarity and agreement.

chapters.n: The Father will gather them and give them Jerusalem as their land of inheritance.
The ruined places of Jerusalem are told to sing for joy, because God has comforted and redeemed his people.

f.w: Sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem

chapters.n: God has “made bare his holy arm,” like a warrior rolling up his sleeve to act. All the earth will see his salvation. Jesus adds that he and the Father are one.

f.w: the Father and I are one

chapters.n: Quoting Isaiah 52:1, Zion is told to awake and put on strength and beautiful garments. Latter-day revelation explains the strength as priesthood power restored to Israel.

f.w: put on thy strength, O Zion

chapters.n: Jerusalem is told to shake off the dust, sit up, and loosen the bands of captivity from her neck — a picture of a prisoner set free.

f.w: loose thyself from the bands of thy neck

chapters.n: Israel “sold itself for nothing” through sin, and will be redeemed without money — through Christ’s grace, not a price paid in silver.
In that day God’s people will know his name and recognize that it is he who speaks. Jesus applies Isaiah’s words directly to himself.

f.w: my people shall know my name

chapters.n: Quoting Isaiah 52:7: how beautiful are the feet of messengers who bring good news and peace, proclaiming “Thy God reigneth.” Abinadi used this verse to describe prophets and Christ himself.
A cry goes out to leave Babylon — the world — and be clean. Those who carry the Lord’s sacred vessels must be pure.

f.w: be ye clean that bear the vessels of the Lord

chapters.n: Unlike the hurried Exodus from Egypt, this gathering will not be in panic. The Lord will lead in front and guard from behind.
Here begins Isaiah’s “suffering servant” passage. The servant will act wisely and be highly exalted — words Christians apply to Christ.
Many were shocked at him because his appearance was marred more than any man’s — a picture of Christ’s suffering.

He will “sprinkle” many nations — cleansing them as a priest sprinkled for purification — and kings will be silenced at what they see. In context, it also points to the marvelous latter-day work of God.

f.w: So shall he sprinkle many nations

chapters.n: Jesus affirms that all of this will surely happen as the Father commanded. The covenant will be fulfilled, and Jerusalem will again be inhabited by his people.
Jesus offers a sign so people can recognize when God is about to gather scattered Israel and establish Zion again. The sign tells when the latter-day gathering begins.

f.w: I give unto you a sign

chapters.n: The sign: when Christ’s words given to these people — essentially the Book of Mormon — are made known to the Gentiles, revealing who Lehi’s descendants are and how the Gentiles scattered them.
These records will come from the Father, through the Gentiles, to the descendants of the people Jesus is addressing. The flow of the message is: Father, Gentiles, then Lehi’s seed.

f.g: From the Gentiles to the descendants of these Nephites and Lamanites.

chapters.n: It is the Father’s wisdom that Gentiles be established in this land as a free people, so the record could come forth from them. Many Latter-day Saints see in this the founding of the United States and its religious liberty.

f.w: set up as a free people

chapters.n: The record will come from the Gentiles to Lehi’s descendants, who will by then have fallen into unbelief because of sin.
Why through Gentiles? So God can show his power to them too, inviting them to repent, be baptized, learn true doctrine, and be counted among Israel. The gospel is for all.

f.w: the true points of my doctrine

chapters.n: When Lehi’s descendants begin to learn these things, it will be a sign that the Father’s work to fulfill his covenant with Israel has already begun.

f.w: the work of the Father hath already commenced

chapters.n: In that day kings will be speechless at what they see and hear — Jesus applies Isaiah 52:15 to the coming forth of this latter-day work.
For Christ’s sake the Father will do a great and marvelous work, yet some will refuse to believe it even when a man declares it to them.

f.w: a great and a marvelous work

chapters.n: God holds his servant’s life in his hand. Though the servant will be “marred,” God will heal him, showing his wisdom is greater than the devil’s cunning. Latter-day Saints often see Joseph Smith in this servant, especially in the loss of the 116 pages.

f.w: my wisdom is greater than the cunning of the devil

chapters.n: Whoever rejects Christ’s words, brought forth to the Gentiles by this servant, will be cut off from the covenant people — as Moses foretold.
Jesus repeats Micah’s image: the remnant of Jacob among the Gentiles will be like a young lion among sheep that no one can stop.

f.w: as a lion among the beasts of the forest

chapters.n: The remnant’s hand will be raised against its enemies, and those enemies cut off. God’s covenant people will ultimately prevail.

f.w: Their hand shall be lifted up

chapters.n: Woe to the Gentiles unless they repent. Now quoting Micah 5:10, God will remove their horses and chariots — the military might they trust in.

f.w: I will cut off thy horses

chapters.n: God will also cut off their cities and throw down their fortresses. Human security systems will not save those who refuse God.
He will remove witchcraft and fortune-telling from the land. False sources of spiritual power and guidance will end.

f.g: Fortune-tellers who claimed to foretell the future.

chapters.n: Idols — carved and standing images — will be removed, and people will no longer worship things they made with their own hands.
God will uproot their “groves” and destroy their cities. Groves were sites of idol worship in the ancient world.

f.g: Sacred poles or tree shrines associated with idol worship (Hebrew asherim).

chapters.n: Lying, deception, envy, strife, priestcraft, and sexual sin will all be done away. Jesus adds this verse to Micah’s list to show the moral cleansing of the last days.

f.g: Preaching for money or praise rather than for God’s glory.

chapters.n: The Father declares that whoever will not repent and come to his Beloved Son will be cut off from his people. Belonging to Israel ultimately depends on coming to Christ.
Severe judgment will fall on the unrepentant, as upon those who never knew God.

f.g: Nations that do not know the true God.

chapters.n: But if the Gentiles repent, God will establish his church among them, bring them into the covenant, and count them with the remnant of Jacob who inherit this land.

f.w: I will establish my church among them

chapters.n: Converted Gentiles will help the remnant of Jacob and gathered Israel build a city called the New Jerusalem.
They will also help gather in God’s scattered people across the land to the New Jerusalem.
Then heaven’s power will come down among them, and Christ himself will be in their midst.

f.w: I also will be in the midst

chapters.n: At that time the Father’s work will begin among all the scattered of Israel, including the lost tribes, as the gospel is preached to the remnant of Lehi’s people.

f.w: the tribes which have been lost

chapters.n: The Father’s work will prepare a way for all scattered Israel to come to Christ and call on the Father in his name. Gathering is first a gathering to Christ.
The work will reach all nations, preparing the way for God’s people to be gathered to their lands of inheritance.
Quoting Isaiah 52:12, they will not flee in haste, for the Lord goes before them and guards their rear. God’s people will be led and protected.

Jesus quotes Isaiah 54 nearly word for word. Israel is pictured as a childless, abandoned wife told to sing, because she will end up with more children than ever — scattered Israel will be gathered in great numbers.
Israel is told to make her tent bigger to hold all her children. Latter-day Saints draw the word “stake” for local church units from this verse — places of strength that hold up the tent of Zion.

f.g: Tent stakes anchor the cords that hold up the tent.

chapters.n: Israel will spread out in every direction, her descendants will inherit the nations, and empty cities will be filled again.

f.w: on the right hand and on the left

chapters.n: Israel need not fear shame any longer; the disgrace of her youth and widowhood will be forgotten. The Book of Mormon text includes an extra line about the “reproach of thy youth” not found in the KJV.
Israel’s Maker is her husband — the Lord of Hosts, her Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, God of the whole earth. Marriage is the image for God’s covenant love.

f.g: Lord of armies — the commander of heaven’s forces.

chapters.n: God has called Israel back like a grieving wife who was rejected in her youth. He takes the initiative to restore the relationship.
God left her only for a brief moment, but he will gather her with great mercy. Compared to eternity, the scattering is short.
In a flash of anger God hid his face briefly, but his kindness and mercy are everlasting. The contrast — a moment versus forever — is the heart of the passage.
As God swore after Noah’s flood never again to flood the earth, he swears he will not stay angry with Israel. His covenant is as sure as the rainbow.
Mountains may move and hills disappear, but God’s kindness and his covenant of peace will never leave his people. This is among the most comforting promises in scripture.
To storm-tossed, uncomforted Israel, God promises to rebuild her with beautiful stones and sapphire foundations — a jeweled city.
Windows of agate, gates of carbuncle, and borders of precious stones describe a glorious, restored Zion, much like the New Jerusalem in Revelation.

f.g: Red gemstones that seem to glow.
Banded, colorful stones; the Hebrew may mean rubies.

chapters.n: All Israel’s children will be taught by the Lord himself and will enjoy great peace. Jesus once quoted this line about those who come to him.
Israel will be established in righteousness, far from oppression and terror. Righteousness brings real security.
Enemies will gather against Israel, but not by God’s will, and they will fall for her sake. God will defend his people.
God made both the blacksmith who forges weapons and the destroyer who uses them. Since he is Creator of all, nothing escapes his control.

f.w: the smith that bloweth the coals
f.g: A blacksmith fanning the fire to make tools or weapons.

chapters.n: No weapon made against God’s people will succeed, and every accusing voice will be refuted. This protection and the righteousness behind it come from the Lord — the inheritance of his servants.

f.w: No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper

chapters.n: Having just quoted Isaiah 54, Jesus commands the people to study Isaiah’s words carefully. Coming from the Savior himself, “great are the words of Isaiah” is a powerful endorsement.

f.w: great are the words of Isaiah

chapters.n: Isaiah spoke about everything concerning Israel, so he necessarily spoke to the Gentiles too, since their stories intertwine in the last days.
Everything Isaiah prophesied has been or will be fulfilled exactly as he said. Isaiah’s prophecies often have more than one fulfillment.
Jesus asks them to write down what he has told them; in the Father’s time it will go to the Gentiles. This is part of how the Book of Mormon came to be.

f.w: write the things which I have told you

chapters.n: Whoever listens, repents, and is baptized will be saved. Jesus also urges them to search all the prophets, because many testify of these same truths.
After explaining all their scriptures, Jesus says there are other scriptures he wants them to write that they don’t yet have.
Jesus asks Nephi to bring the records the people have been keeping. The risen Lord personally reviews their scripture.

f.w: the record which ye have kept

chapters.n: Nephi lays the records before him, and Jesus looks them over.

Jesus reminds them that he commanded Samuel the Lamanite to prophesy that many saints would rise from the dead and minister to many when the Father glorified his name in Christ. He asks, “Was it not so?”

f.w: many saints who should arise from the dead

chapters.n: The disciples confirm Samuel prophesied exactly that and every part was fulfilled.
Jesus asks why they never recorded that the saints rose and ministered to many. The fulfillment of prophecy was missing from the record.
Nephi realizes the fulfillment had not been written down. Even faithful record-keepers can miss important things.
Jesus commands it to be written, and it is. This shows how much the Lord values a complete record of his fulfilled promises.
After explaining all their written scriptures as a unified whole, Jesus commands the disciples to teach what he explained.

f.g: Explained together as one connected whole.

chapters.n: Jesus has the Nephites write Malachi’s words, since Malachi lived after Lehi left Jerusalem and they did not have his book. God promises to send a messenger to prepare the way, and the Lord will suddenly come to his temple.

f.g: The last Old Testament prophet, about 430 BC — well after Lehi left Jerusalem around 600 BC.

chapters.n: Who can endure his coming? He will be like a refiner’s fire that burns away impurities, and like a fuller’s strong soap that scrubs cloth clean.

f.g: Intense heat used to melt metal and separate out the impurities.
A strong cleaner used by a fuller, who washed and whitened new cloth.

chapters.n: The Lord will sit like a silversmith purifying silver, purifying the sons of Levi so they can offer righteous offerings. Latter-day Saints connect this to the restoration of priesthood.
Then the offerings of Judah and Jerusalem will again please the Lord as in earlier, faithful times.

f.w: as in the days of old

chapters.n: God will quickly testify against sorcerers, adulterers, liars, those who cheat workers of wages, oppress widows and orphans, or turn away the foreigner — all who do not fear him.
God does not change. Because he is constant and faithful to his covenant, the children of Jacob have not been destroyed despite their unfaithfulness.
Israel has wandered from God’s ordinances since their ancestors’ time. God invites, “Return unto me and I will return unto you,” but they ask how.

f.w: Return unto me and I will return unto you

chapters.n: God answers: they have robbed him by withholding tithes and offerings. Not giving to God what belongs to him is a kind of theft.

f.g: A tenth of one’s increase given to God.

chapters.n: The whole nation is under a curse because they have robbed God. Their spiritual and material troubles are tied to this neglect.
God invites them to bring all the tithes into the storehouse and test him: he will open heaven’s windows and pour out more blessings than they can hold.

f.g: The temple treasury where offerings were kept.

chapters.n: God will rebuke the “devourer” — pests like locusts — so crops and vines are not ruined. Blessings include protection of what we already have.

f.g: Probably locusts or other crop pests.

chapters.n: All nations will call them blessed, for their land will be delightful. Obedience turns a cursed nation into a blessed one.
God says their words have been harsh against him, yet they ask what they have said.
They complained that serving God is useless, and that obeying and mourning before him brought them no profit. This is the voice of discouraged or cynical believers.

f.w: It is vain to serve God

chapters.n: They even say the proud are happy and the wicked prosper and escape. It is the age-old question of why evil seems to win.

f.w: they that work wickedness are set up

chapters.n: Meanwhile the faithful spoke often to each other, God listened, and a book of remembrance was written for those who feared him. God notices and remembers faithfulness.
These faithful ones will be God’s own treasure when he gathers his jewels, and he will spare them as a father spares a son who serves him.
In the end everyone will see the difference between the righteous and the wicked — between those who serve God and those who don’t. The complaint of verse 15 will be answered.

Continuing with Malachi 4, Jesus describes a coming day that burns like an oven. The proud and wicked will be like dry stubble, consumed completely — “neither root nor branch,” leaving nothing behind.

f.g: Dry stalks left in a field after harvest — they burn instantly.
No ancestors or descendants; often linked to losing eternal family ties.

chapters.n: For those who reverence God, the “Son of Righteousness” will rise with healing in his wings. The KJV reads “Sun,” but the Book of Mormon’s “Son” points directly to Christ. The faithful will grow and leap like well-fed calves let out of the stall.

f.g: Possibly the sun’s rays, or the corners (wings) of a garment; both picture Christ’s healing reach.
Young cattle released from their stall, frisking with energy.

chapters.n: The righteous will triumph over the wicked, who will be like ashes underfoot after that burning day.
Remember the law God gave Moses at Horeb (Mount Sinai). Though Christ fulfilled the law of Moses, Israel is reminded of the covenant foundation God laid there.

God promises to send Elijah the prophet before the great and dreadful day of the Lord. Latter-day Saints believe this was fulfilled when Elijah appeared to Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery in the Kirtland Temple in 1836.

f.g: Great for the righteous, dreadful for the wicked — the Second Coming.

chapters.n: Elijah will turn the hearts of fathers and children toward each other, binding generations together. Latter-day Saints see this in family history and temple sealing work; without it, the earth would be “smitten with a curse.”

f.w: turn the heart of the fathers to the children

chapters.n: After quoting Malachi, Jesus explains everything to the multitude, both the great and the small details. Mormon now begins summarizing rather than quoting.
Jesus says the Father commanded him to give them these scriptures — Malachi’s words — because they would be valuable for future generations, including readers today.
He explains all of history, from the beginning until his glorious return, including the end of this earth when the elements melt and the heavens are rolled up like a scroll.

f.w: elements should melt with fervent heat

f.g: Rolled up like a scroll — the end of the present world.

chapters.n: He also teaches about the Last Judgment, when every person of every nation and language will stand before God and be judged by their works.

f.w: to be judged of their works

chapters.n: The good rise to everlasting life and the evil to damnation — two opposite outcomes. Both flow from the mercy, justice, and holiness of Christ, who existed before the world.

f.g: Set side by side as two opposite paths.

chapters.n: Mormon admits he cannot include even one percent of what Jesus actually taught. The Book of Mormon is a small selection.
The fuller account was on the large plates of Nephi, which Mormon was abridging.

f.g: Here the large plates — the full historical record.

chapters.n: Mormon wrote this smaller portion so that it would come back to Lehi’s descendants through the Gentiles, just as Jesus prophesied.
This lesser part comes first to test people’s faith. If they believe it, God will reveal the greater things. Revelation is given line upon line.
If they won’t believe these things, the greater things will be held back, and they will be condemned for rejecting what they had.
Mormon was about to write everything from the plates of Nephi, but the Lord forbade it, saying he would try the faith of his people.
So Mormon writes only what the Lord commands. He ends his comment and returns to the narrative.
Jesus taught for three days, and afterward appeared often, frequently breaking bread, blessing it, and giving it to them. His ministry among them continued beyond what is recorded in detail.

f.w: for the space of three days

chapters.n: Jesus taught the children and loosened their tongues, and they spoke marvelous things to their parents — things even greater than he had revealed to the adults.
Mormon recaps: after Jesus’ second visit, when he had healed every sickness, opened blind eyes, unstopped deaf ears, raised a man from the dead, and ascended to the Father…

f.w: raised a man from the dead

chapters.n: …the next day the people gathered and heard even babies speak marvelous things. What they said was not allowed to be written.
From then on the twelve disciples baptized and taught everyone who came, and those baptized in Jesus’ name were filled with the Holy Ghost.
Many saw and heard sacred things that were “not lawful” — not permitted — to be written.
The believers taught and served one another, shared everything in common, and dealt honestly with each other — a community much like the early church in Acts.
They did everything exactly as Jesus had commanded. Obedience is the mark of true discipleship.
The baptized believers were called the church of Christ. The church carried the Savior’s name.
Later, as the twelve travel, preach, and baptize, they gather together and unite in powerful prayer and fasting. Their unity sets the stage for another visit from the Lord.
Because they are praying to the Father in his name, Jesus appears among them and asks, “What will ye that I shall give unto you?” He invites them to ask.

f.w: What will ye that I shall give unto you?

chapters.n: They ask what to name the church, since people are arguing about it. Even a name can stir contention.
Jesus asks why people would grumble and argue about this — the answer should be obvious.
The scriptures already teach that believers must take upon them the name of Christ, by which they will be called at the last day.

f.w: take upon you the name of Christ

chapters.n: Those who take his name upon them and endure to the end will be saved. Taking the name is not enough without enduring.
Everything they do should be in Christ’s name: the church should be called by his name, and prayers for the church offered in his name.

f.w: call the church in my name

chapters.n: A church named after Moses would be Moses’ church, and one named after a man would be a man’s church. To be Christ’s church it must bear his name and be built on his gospel — both conditions matter.

f.w: if it so be that they are built upon my gospel

chapters.n: Since they are built on his gospel, whatever they name or do should be in his name; when they pray for the church in his name, the Father will hear.
If the church is built on Christ’s gospel, the Father will show his own works in it — miracles, revelation, and spiritual gifts.
Churches built on human or devilish works may enjoy success for a while, but eventually they are cut down and burned. Lasting joy comes only from what God builds.

f.w: hewn down and cast into the fire

chapters.n: People’s own works follow them and determine their fate. Jesus asks the disciples to remember what he has taught.
Jesus now defines his gospel: he came into the world to do his Father’s will because the Father sent him. This is one of the clearest definitions of the gospel in scripture.

f.w: to do the will of my Father

chapters.n: The Father sent him to be lifted up on the cross, so that he could draw all people to him; just as men lifted him up, the Father will lift all people up — resurrect them — to stand before Christ in judgment.
Through the Father’s power, Christ will draw all people to him to be judged according to their works. The Atonement makes resurrection and judgment universal.
Whoever repents and is baptized in his name will be filled with the Holy Ghost, and those who endure will be held guiltless before the Father when Christ judges the world.
Those who do not endure to the end will be cut down and cannot return, because the Father’s justice must be satisfied.
This is God’s word to all people, and he never lies; he fulfills every word.
No unclean thing can enter God’s kingdom. Only those who have washed their garments in Christ’s blood — through faith, repentance, and faithfulness to the end — enter his rest.

f.w: no unclean thing can enter into his kingdom
washed their garments in my blood

chapters.n: The commandment to the whole world: repent, come to Christ, be baptized in his name, and be sanctified by receiving the Holy Ghost, so as to stand spotless before him at the last day.

f.w: Repent, all ye ends of the earth

chapters.n: “This is my gospel.” The disciples know what to do in his church: do the works they have seen Christ do.

f.w: the works which ye have seen me do

chapters.n: If they do these things, they are blessed and will be lifted up at the last day — exalted with him.
Jesus commands them to write what they have seen and heard, except the sacred things they are forbidden to record.

f.w: save it be those which are forbidden

chapters.n: They should also write the future acts of this people, just as past events have been recorded.
People will be judged out of the books written about them, because those records show their works.
The Father himself records all things, so the world will be judged from what is written.
The twelve will be judges of this people, using the just judgment Christ gives them. Then the great question: what kind of people should they be? “Even as I am.”

f.w: ye shall be judges of this people
what manner of men ought ye to be? Verily I say unto you, even as I am

chapters.n: Jesus is going to the Father, and promises that whatever they ask the Father in his name will be given.

f.w: ask the Father in my name

chapters.n: Ask, receive; knock, and the door opens. God responds to those who seek him.
Jesus says his joy is full because of them and this generation; the Father and angels rejoice too, because none of them are lost.

f.w: my joy is great, even unto fulness

chapters.n: He clarifies that he means those now living in this generation — none are lost, and in them he has fulness of joy.
But he grieves for the fourth generation, who will be led captive by Satan like Judas and will sell Christ for silver, gold, and things that decay. Fourth Nephi and Mormon record this tragic decline.
Jesus ends with the image of two gates: the narrow one leads to life and few find it; the wide one leads to death, traveled by many until the night comes when no one can work.

f.w: Enter ye in at the strait gate
the night cometh, wherein no man can work

chapters.n: Jesus asks each of the twelve, one at a time, what they want from him after he returns to the Father. It is a personal, open invitation.
Nine of them ask that after a full lifetime of service they may quickly come to him in his kingdom. It is a righteous desire to finish their work and be with the Lord.
Jesus blesses them for this wish and promises that at age seventy-two they will come to him and find rest.
Then Jesus turns to the remaining three and asks what they want.
The three are sorrowful and afraid to say what they want. Their wish seems too bold to voice.
Jesus knows their thoughts: they want what John the Beloved wanted — to stay on earth and keep bringing souls to Christ.
They are “more blessed” and will never die; they will witness God’s dealings with humanity until Christ returns in glory.
They will not suffer death’s pains. When Christ comes, they will be changed in an instant from mortal to immortal.

f.w: in the twinkling of an eye

chapters.n: They will feel no physical pain and sorrow only for the world’s sins. All this is granted because their desire is to bring souls to Christ while the world lasts.

f.w: save it be for the sins of the world

chapters.n: Because of this they will have fulness of joy and sit in the Father’s kingdom, becoming like Christ as he is like the Father.

f.w: ye shall be even as I am
the Father and I are one

chapters.n: The Holy Ghost testifies of the Father and the Son, and the Father gives the Holy Ghost to people because of Christ.
Jesus touches the nine with his finger — not the three who will remain — and then departs.

f.w: touched every one of them with his finger

chapters.n: Now Mormon writes about the three: heaven opens, they are caught up, and they see and hear indescribable things.
They are forbidden to tell what they saw, and they are not even given the ability to describe it.
They cannot tell whether they were in or out of their bodies. It seemed like a transfiguration — a change to an immortal state so they could see the things of God.

f.w: whether they were in the body or out of the body

f.g: A temporary change by God’s power enabling a person to endure his presence.

chapters.n: They return to minister on earth, but do not reveal what they experienced in heaven.
Mormon honestly says he doesn’t yet know whether they became mortal or immortal after that day. He later receives an answer (verses 36-40).
What he does know is that they ministered everywhere, brought believers into the church through baptism, and those baptized received the Holy Ghost.
Unbelievers threw them into prison, but the prisons could not hold them — they split apart.

f.w: the prisons could not hold them

chapters.n: Thrown into pits in the earth, they “smote the earth with the word of God” and were delivered. No pit could hold them.
Three times they were thrown into a furnace without harm, like Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
Twice thrown to wild beasts, they played with them like a child with a lamb — recalling Daniel in the lions’ den and Isaiah’s vision of peace.

f.g: A very young lamb still nursing.

chapters.n: They preached Christ to all the Nephites, and the people were converted and united to the church, fulfilling Jesus’ words about that generation.

f.w: according to the word of Jesus

chapters.n: Mormon pauses his account of the three disciples for now.
He was about to record their names, but the Lord forbade it. They are hidden from the world.
Mormon personally testifies he has seen the three and they ministered to him.
They will be among the Gentiles, unrecognized.
They will be among the Jews, unrecognized as well.
When the Lord chooses, they will minister to scattered Israel and all nations, bringing many souls to Jesus, fulfilling their desire through the convincing power of God within them.
They are like angels: by praying to the Father in Jesus’ name, they can show themselves to anyone they choose.
They will perform great and marvelous works before the day when everyone stands before Christ’s judgment seat.
Even among the Gentiles they will do a great and marvelous work before judgment day.
If we had all the scriptures recording Christ’s works, we would know these things must surely happen. The written record is incomplete, but Christ’s word is sure.
Woe to those who reject Jesus’ words and those of his chosen servants. To reject them is to reject him, and he will not receive such people at the last day.
It would be better for them not to have been born. Mormon asks: do you think you can escape the justice of a God whom men trampled underfoot so that salvation could come?

f.w: better for them if they had not been born

chapters.n: Mormon returns to his question about whether the three were changed from mortality to immortality.
Since writing, he has asked the Lord and learned that their bodies had to be changed, or they would have to die. Here we see Mormon receiving revelation while he writes.

f.w: I have inquired of the Lord

chapters.n: So their bodies were changed, freeing them from pain and from all sorrow except for the sins of the world.

f.w: a change wrought upon their bodies

chapters.n: This change was not yet resurrection, but it put them beyond Satan’s power to tempt, made them holy in the flesh, and freed them from earthly restraints. Latter-day Saints call such beings “translated.”

f.g: Made holy while still in a physical body — often called being translated.

f.w: Satan could have no power over them

chapters.n: They will stay in this state until Christ’s judgment day, then receive a greater change — resurrection — and dwell with God forever.

Mormon speaks directly to latter-day readers: when this record reaches the Gentiles, you can know that God’s covenant to restore Israel to its lands is already being fulfilled. The Book of Mormon itself is the sign.

f.w: these sayings shall come unto the Gentiles

chapters.n: All the prophets’ words will be fulfilled. No one should claim the Lord is delaying his promises to Israel.
Don’t imagine that the prophecies were empty words. The Lord will remember his covenant with Israel.
When this record appears, stop mocking the Lord’s works. His sword of justice is in his right hand, and judgment will quickly overtake those who scorn him.
Woe to anyone who scorns the Lord’s works or denies Christ and his deeds.
Woe to those who deny revelation and claim God no longer works through prophecy, spiritual gifts, tongues, healing, or the Holy Ghost. Mormon foresaw the modern idea that miracles ended long ago.

f.w: the Lord no longer worketh by revelation

chapters.n: Woe to those who, for profit, say Christ can work no miracles. Such a person becomes like the son of perdition, who received no mercy.
Stop hissing at, scorning, or mocking the Jews or any remnant of Israel. The Lord remembers his covenant with them and will do what he swore.

f.g: Make a scornful sound of contempt.

chapters.n: No one can turn God’s right hand to his left — that is, reverse his purposes. He will judge and fulfill his covenant with Israel.

f.w: turn the right hand of the Lord unto the left
f.g: An idiom for undoing or thwarting God’s plans.

chapters.n: Mormon closes 3 Nephi by delivering a message Jesus commanded him to write to the Gentiles of the last days. He introduces it as the words of Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God.

f.w: the Son of the living God

chapters.n: Christ calls the Gentiles to turn from lying, deception, sexual sin, secret evils, idolatry, murder, priestcraft, envy, and strife; to come to him and be baptized for remission of sins; to be filled with the Holy Ghost; and to be counted among Israel. It is a one-verse summary of the gospel invitation.

f.g: Preaching for money or popularity instead of God’s glory.
